source.title: Understanding and Improving Group Normalization
source.authors: Agus Gunawan; Xu Yin; Kang Zhang

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices. Some reported results are figure-only; numerical values are not available in text for those figures.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures training behavior and optimization stability with and without normalization, and reports training-performance results for GN on several network families. It does not test the claim’s specific CIFAR training-error outcomes, but its results bear on V3 and V6’s training claims using different metrics and methods.
record.gate_note: Reports training and validation performance for GN versus networks without normalization in ResNet, DenseNet, and VGG, and reports normalization comparisons using loss landscape, gradient predictiveness, and validation accuracy. The paper’s cited results from other studies are not rows. CIFAR accuracy tables concern validation accuracy, not training classification error.
record.test_reason: The study uses BN's presumed optimization benefits to design a GN/BN hybrid. Its own results concern GN, hybrid-method performance, endpoint validation accuracy, and optimization diagnostics. It does not measure BN versus no normalization on accuracy-gain speed or learning-rate tolerance, or test any other claim version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: GN is sensitive to output distortion and regularization, helps slightly in the middle of training, and harms early training according to their diagnostics. They attribute hybrid improvements to incorporating BN and report better aggregate performance than GN. Their conclusions require the stated qualifications: some hybrid variants explode, GNPlusGNFirst fails in a small-batch SVHN setting, and its reported aggregate advantage excludes that failure. BN achieves the best classification-table results.
record.recipe_differences: Uses normalization comparisons and optimization diagnostics rather than the claim versions' interventions; proposes an adaptive BN/GN hybrid. The paper reports CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: GN's reported performance varies by training period, learning rate, regularization and batch size. GNPlusGNFirst has gradient-explosion failures for some variants and small-batch SVHN settings.

fits_no_version.finding: GN reportedly improves training and validation performance over unnormalized ResNet50, DenseNet121, and VGG-11.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Group normalization can improve training in several convolutional architecture families.

fits_no_version.finding: GN has wider loss-landscape and gradient-predictiveness ranges than BN, performs worse than no normalization early in training, and becomes more sensitive under weight decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GN's optimization diagnostics depend on training phase and regularization and are less favorable than BN's in these VGG-11 experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: BN has higher endpoint validation accuracy than GN at every reported batch size on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BN outperforms GN on endpoint validation accuracy in the tested ResNet50 recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: GNPlusGNFirst improves reported mean validation accuracy and optimization diagnostics over GN, but individual conditions do not uniformly improve and small-batch SVHN training can fail.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An adaptive GN/BN hybrid can improve GN's aggregate performance with setting-dependent benefits and failures.

fits_no_version.finding: Injected Gaussian output noise causes reported gradient vanishing with GN, while BN and GNPlusGNFirst avoid that failure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization methods differ in robustness to injected output-distribution distortion.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A.5 reports settings where BN trains successfully while GN suffers gradient vanishing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BN and GN differ in training robustness for particular VGG-11 learning-rate and batch-size combinations.

record.problems: Training metrics and loss-landscape results are largely reported in figures without exact values. The CIFAR tables report validation accuracy, not training classification error. Some hybrid variants fail with gradient explosion, and some results are excluded from reported best-result comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for row limit. Figures 5, 10 and 11 report additional noise and regularization comparisons, but the direct result rows retained above prioritize outcomes relevant to the claim versions. Appendix A.5's exploratory GBGN/BGN and stacked-layer results are not rows because they test other methods, not the claim's named interventions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and model-size or training-recipe qualifications.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation across depth, prevention by identity shortcuts, and the initialization exceptions.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, learning speed, and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to a stability threshold, curvature trajectories, recovery, and divergence.
BN versus no normalization on accuracy-gain speed and higher learning-rate tolerance; Fixup's normalization-free training comparison.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are warranted for the supplied versions. Optimization diagnostics cannot substitute for measured accuracy-gain speed. The batch-size experiments also scale learning rate with batch size, so they do not isolate batch-size sensitivity. Figure curves are unavailable in the supplied text; textual summaries do not establish additional version-specific outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training classification error for sufficiently large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, model size, or early stopping.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem or neuron-width sweep.
Tests GN’s effect on training behavior in different network families, including ResNet, but does not compare plain versus identity-shortcut networks across depth or measure training error by depth.
Does not compare initialization methods or test trainable depth.
Does not test learning rates relative to a stability limit, curvature thresholds, or recovery versus divergence.

Tests normalization comparisons on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN and training metrics in VGG-11; does not test sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10 or Inception ImageNet accuracy-gain speed as specified, nor Fixup.

rows.subject: VGG-11
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss landscape and gradient predictiveness when trained with GN versus BN.

conditions.value: five values from 10−4 until 5 × 10−4 with an increment of 10−4

rows.measure: Loss landscape and gradient predictiveness; lower values and smaller ranges indicate better training performance.
rows.value: GN has wider ranges and higher minimum loss-landscape values, especially in the initial training period; gradient predictiveness follows a similar trend.
rows.note: This result challenges the claim that adding BN improves training in these tested conditions only in that GN performs worse than BN; it does not measure accuracy gain over training time.
rows.check: Loss-landscape ranges and gradient predictiveness comparing GN with BN do not measure V6's accuracy-gain speed or learning-rate tolerance. GN performing worse than BN is not a reversal of V6.

rows.check: Regularization sensitivity of optimization diagnostics is a different outcome from V6's training-speed and learning-rate claims.
